clue.text: Remarkably neat, trim disciplinarian

indicators.note: remarkably suggests the letters of neat and trim behave out of the ordinary, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A strict boss who keeps themselves remarkably neat and trim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Remarkably' looks like praise of a tidy person, but it signals that NEAT and TRIM are mixed into one eight-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: A martinet is a strict enforcer of rules, named after a French army drillmaster.

clue.text: A Spaniard is a handsome man

parts.note: Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman, so a Spaniard
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone claims that a particular Spaniard is very good-looking.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Adonis was a youth of great beauty, so his name stands for any good-looking fellow.

clue.text: In panto, scant role for opera singer

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the run of words panto scant

explanation.surface: A pantomime offers only a meagre part to a performer from the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across the end of 'panto' and the start of 'scant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's opera has a title heroine, a soprano part sung by many famous divas.

clue.text: Hang on less tightly

explanation.surface: Advice to grip something more loosely.
explanation.definitionFit: Wait a moment is said to slow someone down; read literally, the phrase means with less firmness or tightness.

clue.text: Incline to be unwell internally-it's the back

indicators.note: internally tells us the sickness sits within the leaning word

parts.note: to incline towards something is to tend
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: Someone who tends to feel ill in the middle blames it on their back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incline' looks like a slope and 'the back' like a body part; here it means the last part of something, and 'it's' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear part of something, such as a queue or a procession, is its last section.

clue.text: Laid back about sergeant major causing depression

indicators.note: about means the turned word wraps around the soldier
back means the word laid is read from its end to its start

parts.note: taken as written
SM is the usual military abbreviation for sergeant major

explanation.surface: A laid-back attitude towards the sergeant major leads to a gloomy mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the first word into DIAL; 'Laid back' looks like a relaxed attitude, but 'back' acts only on 'Laid'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dreary and gloomy brings on low spirits.

clue.text: Takes out some fruit

explanation.surface: A person takes someone out for a meal involving fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: To court someone is to go on outings with them; the sweet brown fruit of a palm tree is another sense.

clue.text: Extra burden for fish caught in swell

indicators.note: caught in pictures the fish trapped inside the wave

parts.note: a surge is a swell of the sea
char is a fish related to the trout

explanation.surface: A fish swept up in a big wave adds to a load.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swell' looks like a verb but is a noun, the rising of the sea; char is a cold-water fish of the trout family.
explanation.definitionFit: An additional charge or load placed on top of the usual one.

clue.text: Purloin a modern painting

explanation.surface: Someone steals a piece of contemporary art.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstract can mean to remove or steal; non-representational art of the twentieth century is another sense.

clue.text: Stays determined to pursue the French horn

indicators.note: to pursue means the determined word follows behind the horn

parts.note: cor is the French word for horn
set means determined, as in set on doing something

explanation.surface: Someone resolved to chase after a French brass instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stays' is a noun: the bones of a laced undergarment, and so the garment itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Stays is an old word for a stiffened, laced bodice worn to shape the waist.

clue.text: Return enthusiasm

explanation.surface: A two-word note about getting back keen feelings.
explanation.definitionFit: Money earned on savings is a yield or gain; keen curiosity about something is another sense.

clue.text: Protective clothing commanded by Corcoran

explanation.surface: Overalls handed out by someone called Corcoran.
explanation.walkthrough: In Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera HMS Pinafore, Captain Corcoran commands the ship.
explanation.definitionFit: An apron-like garment worn over clothes; also the name of the ship in the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta.

clue.text: A painter has returned from the desert

indicators.note: returned means the pieces together are read from end to start

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is a painter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A painter has come back from the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns the whole run ARAHAS round; RA stands for a Royal Academician, a member of London's Royal Academy of Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: The great desert of North Africa, the largest hot desert on Earth.

clue.text: The finest area to be a National Park

parts.note: at its peak means at its finest
a district is an area

explanation.surface: Praising the best area as worthy of being a protected national park.
explanation.definitionFit: A hilly upland in England's Midlands was the first area made a protected park, in 1951.

clue.text: Royal person not up at university

parts.note: a prince is a royal person

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word not is read bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A royal who has not gone up to university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns NOT into TON. 'Up' looks like the British 'go up to university', which fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An Ivy League college in New Jersey, one of the oldest in the USA.

clue.text: New town still in process of development

indicators.note: in places the adverb within the phase word

parts.note: a stage is a step in a process of development
even and still both strengthen a comparison: even better, still better

explanation.surface: A new town is still being built and developed.
explanation.walkthrough: Stevenage, in Hertfordshire, was the first of Britain's post-war planned New Towns, so 'New town' is a fair definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This Hertfordshire place was the first planned settlement designated under the UK's 1946 New Towns Act.

clue.text: Form view the hill has nothing inside

indicators.note: inside means the zero sits within the two words joined

parts.note: taken as written
a rise is a small hill
O, the figure zero, means nothing

explanation.surface: Someone forms an opinion that the hill is hollow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form view' reads like a noun phrase but is a verb: to form a view.
explanation.definitionFit: To speculate is to work out an idea or opinion.

clue.text: Day before the present day?

parts.note: reads as yesterday, but the present is a gift: the day before gifts are opened on the twenty-fifth of December

explanation.surface: Asking what we call yesterday.
explanation.definitionFit: The twenty-fourth of December precedes the festive day when gifts are given.

clue.text: A job given to the French missionary

parts.note: a post is a job
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A missionary is given a job in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Early Christian teachers sent out to spread the faith were missionaries.

clue.text: I'd best move living quarters

indicators.note: move tells us to shift the letters of I'd best around

explanation.surface: Someone decides they had better move to a new place to live.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' fits the house-hunting surface, but it rearranges I'D BEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A single rented room used for both sleeping and living.

clue.text: Agree to study dog

parts.note: to con is an old word meaning to study or learn
a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: Someone agrees to make a study of a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: To be of the same mind is to agree.

clue.text: Serving of sandwiches-not this shape surely?

definitions.text: Serving of sandwiches-not this shape surely?

parts.words: Serving of sandwiches-not this shape surely?
parts.note: a serving of sandwiches has a special name, and the clue jokes that sandwiches are cut square or triangular, never circular

explanation.surface: Wondering what shape sandwiches really ought to be.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a set of sandwiches made from two slices of bread is one portion; the word also names a circular shape.

clue.text: Pass mark?

parts.note: not an exam score: to pass beyond a line or mark is to go too far

explanation.surface: Asking about the score needed to pass a test.
explanation.definitionFit: To go beyond acceptable limits, as in going over the mark.

clue.text: Hard back

explanation.surface: A two-word description of a tough rear.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe or strict is one sense; the rear part of a ship is another.

clue.text: Suspicion that damp leads to corrosion

parts.note: mist is damp air, and leads to places it first, ahead of the corrosion word
rust is corrosion of iron

explanation.surface: Doubts about whether damp conditions cause metal to rust.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of trust and suspicion are the same feeling.

clue.text: Parade-ground command is a joke

parts.note: to tease is to joke with someone; a tease is a joke

explanation.surface: Someone says a drill order is laughable.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces make A TEASE, the same letters as the command split differently.
explanation.definitionFit: The order to stand relaxed, feet apart, is shouted on the drill square.

clue.text: Wrote in prison?

explanation.surface: Wondering if someone wrote while locked up.
explanation.definitionFit: To write with a pen is one sense; to be shut up in an enclosure, as in a pen, is another.

clue.text: Sort of ring for a long time

explanation.surface: Describing a ring that lasts for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: A band of stones set all round is one kind of ring; endless or very long duration is the other sense.
